claims.claim: Moniz initiated the first leucotomy on 12 November 1935 at the Hospital de Santa Marta in Lisbon.
claims.episode_span: On a November morning in 1935, António Egas Moniz watched as a surgeon drilled two small holes into the skull of a sixty-three-year-old woman at Lisbon’s Santa Marta Hospital
claims.supporting_quote: [ 60 ] Development [ edit ] The pioneer of lobotomies, the Portuguese neurologist and Nobel Laureate António Egas Moniz Leucotomy was first undertaken in 1935 under the direction of the Portuguese neurologist (and inventor of the term psychosurgery ) António Egas Moniz .

claims.claim: Moniz was awarded the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for leucotomy, shared with Swiss physiologist Walter Rudolf Hess.
claims.episode_span: António Egas Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize for the prefrontal lobotomy
claims.supporting_quote: Because the procedure met with seemingly widespread success, Moniz was awarded the 1949 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine (along with Swiss physiologist Walter Rudolf Hess ).

claims.claim: In Moniz's published assessment of his first twenty patients, seven improved significantly and seven were somewhat improved (fourteen total), with no deaths reported.
claims.episode_span: Moniz published his first series of twenty patients in 1936, reporting improvement in fourteen cases with relatively few immediate deaths.
claims.supporting_quote: the outcome for these first twenty patients was that 35%, or seven cases, improved significantly, another 35% were somewhat improved and the remaining 30% (six cases) were unchanged

claims.claim: Walter Freeman performed the first transorbital lobotomy in the United States on 17 January 1946, on Sallie Ellen Ionesco, in his Washington, D.C. office.
claims.episode_span: he performed the first American transorbital lobotomy on 17 January 1946
claims.supporting_quote: Jan. 17, 1946: Walter Freeman performs the first transorbital lobotomy in the United States on a 29-year-old housewife named Sallie Ellen Ionesco in his Washington, D.C., office.

claims.claim: About 50,000 people received lobotomies in the United States.
claims.episode_span: Roughly 50,000 lobotomies are estimated to have been performed in the United States between 1936 and 1956.
claims.source_title: Frequently Asked Questions About Lobotomies : NPR
claims.supporting_quote: About 50,000 people received lobotomies in the United States, most of them between 1949 and 1952. About 10,000 of these procedures were transorbital lobotomies.

claims.claim: Nearly 60% of American lobotomy patients were women, per a 1951 study.
claims.episode_span: Women received a disproportionate share of operations — roughly 60 percent of documented cases
claims.supporting_quote: More lobotomies were performed on women than on men: a 1951 study found that nearly 60% of American lobotomy patients were women

claims.claim: The introduction of chlorpromazine (Thorazine) in 1954 ended the era of widespread hospital psychosurgery.
claims.episode_span: The introduction of chlorpromazine in 1954 provided a reversible pharmacological alternative and sharply reduced the number of new lobotomies
claims.supporting_quote: 1954: Era of widespread hospital psychosurgery fades away with introduction of chlorpromazine (Thorazine).

claims.claim: Freeman performed his last transorbital lobotomy in February 1967, on longtime patient Helen Mortensen.
claims.episode_span: Freeman continued performing the transorbital variant until 1967, but most hospitals quietly withdrew support.
claims.supporting_quote: February 1967: Freeman performs his last transorbital lobotomy on a longtime patient, Helen Mortensen.
